checks.prompt: A studio needs two things: rolling hills whose height varies smoothly across a continent, and a city grid whose roads always connect and never dead-end into a building. A programmer proposes this algorithm for both, on the grounds that it is 'the procedural generation algorithm'. Assess.
checks.explanation: The dividing line is discrete-and-rule-bound versus continuous-and-smooth. Roads, pipes and rooms are the former; terrain height and clouds are the latter. The second half of the answer is the caveat that catches people who do choose it correctly: the rules it enforces are between neighbours, so a global property like 'every room is reachable' is not implied and has to be added or checked separately.
options: It is right for the second and wrong for the first. This algorithm fills a grid of discrete choices subject to which choices may sit next to which, which is exactly a road network with connection rules; a continuous height field that varies smoothly has no discrete tiles and no adjacency table, and is what gradient noise is for. And even for the second, the guarantee is local: adjacency rules cannot by themselves promise that the whole network is connected
It is right for both: the height field is generated by using a very large tile set of height values, and the adjacency rules then enforce smoothness
It is wrong for both: it produces only textures that imitate an example image, so neither a height field nor a functional road layout is within its scope
It is right for the first and wrong for the second: smooth fields are its strength, while discrete layouts with connection rules require a dedicated constraint solver

checks.prompt: A first implementation picks the next cell to decide uniformly at random instead of by remaining uncertainty. It works on small grids and fails constantly on large ones. Explain the two-move loop the algorithm runs, why the choice of which cell to decide next matters so much, and what the failure actually is.
checks.explanation: The heuristic is the algorithm's whole reliability story: decide where you are least free, so the decision is nearly forced and the chance of painting yourself into a corner stays low. Uniform choice keeps the same rules and loses that property entirely.
checks.expected: A correct answer must describe both moves and the heuristic. The loop alternates deciding and consequences. Deciding: pick a cell that is not yet resolved and commit it to one of the options it still has, chosen at random with a bias toward more frequent options. Consequences: that commitment makes some options impossible for its neighbours, so those are removed; removing them may in turn make options impossible for their neighbours, and the removals are pushed outward until nothing more changes — this is ordinary constraint propagation, and it is what turns one local decision into a global narrowing. Why the order matters: committing where you have the most freedom is committing where you have the least information, and the commitment is arbitrary; committing instead where the fewest options remain means the decision is nearly forced anyway, so it is far less likely to be inconsistent with what the rest of the grid will need. Choosing uniformly scatters arbitrary commitments across a wide-open grid, and their consequences eventually meet in the middle and disagree. The failure is a cell whose option set becomes empty — no value is compatible with its already-decided surroundings — at which point there is nothing to do but undo recent decisions or start the grid again, and on a large grid a restart throws away a lot of work. Noting that the proper measure of a cell's uncertainty is the entropy of its weighted options rather than the raw count, and that ties are broken randomly, is a plus.

checks.prompt: Two ways to obtain the adjacency table are offered. One asks the author to state which tiles may neighbour which; the other takes a single small example image, extracts every square patch of a fixed size, and declares two patches compatible when their overlap agrees. What distinguishes them in practice?
checks.explanation: One is authored, the other is extracted. Authoring gives you rules you can read, argue about and edit, which matters when the constraints encode a design intent. Extraction gives you a style from one picture with no rule-writing at all — the thing that makes the algorithm feel magical — but the resulting pattern set is large and effectively opaque. Neither involves training in the machine-learning sense.
options: The first gives explicit, auditable control over a hand-designed tile set, which is what you want when the rules are a design decision — a pipe must connect to a pipe. The second requires no rule authoring at all: the style is inferred from one picture, so the output is locally indistinguishable from the example without anyone writing a rule, at the cost of rules you cannot easily inspect or edit and a much larger set of patterns
The first is faster to run and the second is slower, but they produce identical outputs from equivalent inputs, so the choice is purely about authoring convenience
The second requires a training phase over many example images, which is what makes its rules richer; the first works from a single example without training
The first works only for square tiles and the second only for hexagonal ones, so the choice is determined by the grid's geometry

checks.prompt: Implement the consequences half of the loop. Write `propagate(domains, neighbours, allowed, seeds)`. `domains` maps each cell to the set of values it may still take. `neighbours` maps a cell to `{direction: other_cell}`. `allowed` maps a direction to `{value: set of values permitted in that direction from it}`; a value absent from that table permits nothing. `seeds` lists the cells whose options have just changed. Starting from the seeds, repeatedly enforce that every value remaining in a neighbour is supported — that is, permitted in that direction by at least one value still available in the cell — removing unsupported values and queueing any neighbour whose set actually shrank, until nothing more changes. Return a NEW mapping, leaving the input untouched. Raise `ValueError` if any cell begins with an empty set, if a seed or a neighbour names a cell absent from `domains`, or if enforcing support would leave a cell with no values at all. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Two properties of the propagation are visible here and both matter. First, the ripple stops on its own: it re-queues a cell only when that cell's option set actually shrank, so a neighbour that loses nothing ends the chain, which is why deciding one cell in a permissive grid barely disturbs anything while deciding one in a tight grid can cascade across the whole line. Second, the failure it reports is not necessarily where the decision was made — the chain case fails two cells away from anything that was collapsed, and that is exactly why the algorithm cannot simply check the cell it just decided. Returning a new mapping rather than editing in place is what makes undoing a decision possible at all.

checks.prompt: A dungeon generator using this algorithm produces layouts that always obey the tile rules, but roughly one map in five has a treasure room walled off from the rest, and about one run in twelve fails outright after exhausting its retries. A designer proposes making the adjacency rules stricter to fix both. Assess.
checks.explanation: Two problems pulling in opposite directions. The rules are local by construction, so a global property like connectivity is outside what they can say, and it has to be verified or repaired separately. And every constraint you add removes consistent solutions, so a tighter rule set raises the failure rate — which is why the two proposals cannot both be served by the same change.
options: Stricter rules will make the second problem worse and will not fix the first. Reachability is a property of the whole map, and rules that only say which tiles may be adjacent cannot express it — so it needs either a check-and-regenerate pass, a post-processing step that carves a connection, or an extra global constraint. Meanwhile tightening the rules shrinks the space of consistent layouts, which makes the solver run into unsatisfiable states more often, not less
Stricter rules fix both, because a rule set that forbids isolated wall configurations makes disconnection impossible and also removes the ambiguity that causes failures
Both problems indicate the retry limit is too low; raising it resolves the failures, and the disconnected rooms are an artefact of aborted runs being reported as successes
The disconnection is expected and cannot be addressed at all, while the failures indicate the tile set is too small and should be expanded with rotated variants

checks.prompt: Four tasks. (1) Cloud cover for a weather visualisation. (2) A 40 by 40 tilemap in the visual style of one hand-drawn 16 by 16 example, with no rules written by hand. (3) A puzzle layout that must satisfy hard global requirements — exactly three keys, every door reachable, a guaranteed solution — over a large space. (4) A pipe-network puzzle where connectors must join and the designer wants to pre-place a few tiles and bias others. Recommend and justify each.
checks.explanation: Two of the four are this algorithm, in its two different forms, and the split between them is whether the rules are authored or inferred. The other two mark its boundaries: continuous fields on one side and hard global guarantees on the other.
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all four with a decisive property. (1) Gradient noise: the output is a smooth continuous field with no discrete alphabet of tiles and no notion of which value may sit beside which — the deciding property is continuity, and imposing a tile grammar on it would be an odd way to obtain smoothness. (2) This algorithm in its example-driven form: the patch-extraction variant learns the adjacency rules from a single image, which is precisely the requirement that no rules be authored, and the output will be locally indistinguishable from the example while being globally new — the deciding property is that the style is defined by an example rather than by rules. (3) A dedicated constraint or satisfiability solver: hard global requirements such as exact counts and guaranteed reachability are outside what neighbour rules express, and a solver with backtracking and global constraints will both express them and search the space properly — the deciding property is that the requirements are global and must hold, not merely be likely. (4) This algorithm in its hand-authored form: connector matching is a design decision that belongs in explicit rules, and the two extras asked for are natively supported — pre-placing tiles is just starting some cells already decided, and biasing is what the option weights do — the deciding property is controllability over rules that a person is writing on purpose. Noting that a large space with very tight rules pushes even the right choice toward backtracking or a hierarchical formulation rather than restart-on-failure is a plus.
